opus-5.5.text:
I think about it less as "real versus sim" and more as which data teaches the robot what.

Real-robot data is the gold standard for one reason: it's the actual distribution you deploy into. The contact dynamics, the friction, a cable snagging, a cloth folding in a slightly unexpected way. Those are exactly where simulators are weakest. If you want a robot to fold laundry or handle deformable objects, there's really no substitute for real interaction. The problem is that it's expensive and slow. Every demonstration takes a human operator, hardware time, resets, and the hardware breaks. So you hit a scaling wall pretty quickly.

Simulation is the opposite. It's nearly free to scale, you can parallelize thousands of environments, randomize everything, and run reinforcement learning without worrying about breaking anything. For locomotion it has been incredibly successful. Legged robots trained almost entirely in sim now transfer well, because rigid-body dynamics and the robot's own body are things we can model reasonably accurately. But once you get into rich manipulation, with lots of contact, soft materials, and visual diversity, the sim-to-real gap becomes the bottleneck. You can spend more effort building a faithful simulator than you would have spent just collecting the data.

So my practical view is something like this. Use simulation where the physics is well understood and where you need massive exploration, like low-level control, locomotion, and pretraining certain skills. Use real data for the parts where the world is messy and where the behavior you care about lives in that messiness. And increasingly there's a middle ground: cheaper ways of collecting real-world data, like handheld grippers or human videos, that aren't full teleoperation but still capture real physics and real diversity.

If I had to put a weight on it for general-purpose manipulation today, I'd lean toward real data being the core and sim being the supplement. That ratio could shift as simulators and generative world models get better. But I'd be cautious about betting everything on closing the sim-to-real gap, because the long tail of the real world is exactly what's hardest to simulate.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts real data’s high cost and slow collection with simulation’s cheap, scalable volume, while explaining that real data better captures messy contact and simulation can have a transfer gap in rich manipulation.

r002.rationale: It says there is “really no substitute for real interaction” for laundry and deformable objects, and that the sim-to-real gap becomes a bottleneck in rich manipulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as a trade-off where you pick one. They answer different questions, and the mistake most teams make is trying to get one source to do the other's job.

Real-robot data is the only thing that tells you the truth about the world. Contact dynamics, deformable objects, lighting that changes at four in the afternoon, a gripper that's slightly worn — none of that shows up in a simulator unless you already knew to model it, and the whole point is that you don't. So real data is irreplaceable for grounding. The problem is it's brutally expensive. You need hardware, operators, teleoperation rigs, and every hour of data costs you a real hour of a real machine, plus the breakdowns. And the distribution is narrow. You collect what your few robots happened to see.

Simulation is the opposite profile. It's cheap, it's parallel, you can get millions of episodes overnight, and you can deliberately push into rare or dangerous situations you'd never want to run on hardware. Where it fails is physics fidelity and visual realism. For something like locomotion or navigation, sim has basically won — the gap is small enough that you can train almost entirely in sim and transfer with a bit of randomization. For dexterous manipulation, especially anything involving contact-rich tasks, cloth, liquids, or small parts, the sim-to-real gap is still real, and I've watched policies that look perfect in sim fall apart the moment they touch a physical object.

So the way I actually weigh it is by task. The more the task depends on contact physics and perception of messy stuff, the more I lean on real data. The more it depends on long-horizon planning, coverage of edge cases, or motor skills with clean dynamics, the more I lean on sim.

And then the thing that matters most is using them together. Real data is the anchor — it tells you where your simulator is wrong, so you can calibrate it. Sim gives you the breadth and the safety. Right now I think a reasonable ratio for a manipulation stack is a relatively small amount of high-quality real demonstrations, maybe tens of thousands of episodes, used to ground a model that's been pretrained on much larger sim and video-derived data. Over time I expect the real-data requirement per task keeps shrinking, because foundation models are getting better at transferring priors. But I don't expect it to go to zero. Somebody always has to pay the cost of touching the world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts real data’s high cost and narrow coverage with simulation’s scale, and discusses task-dependent effectiveness. But it rejects framing the choice as a tradeoff and does not state the specific quantity-versus-model-improvement framing in the criterion.

r002.rationale: It says simulation policies for contact-rich manipulation can fail when they encounter physical objects, and that real data is needed to ground them.

astra-6.text:
I think they play complementary roles. Simulation gives you scale: you can vary environments, repeat tasks, and explore failures without damaging hardware. But a robot can get very good at exploiting the simulator’s assumptions, so success there doesn’t necessarily mean success in the real world.

Real-robot data tells you what you’re missing—things like contact, friction, sensor noise, and delays. It’s more expensive to collect, so I’d use it strategically: to ground the training, identify where the simulated behavior breaks down, and test whether improvements actually transfer.

So I wouldn’t aim for a fixed ratio. I’d ask, for this particular task, what’s limiting performance? If it’s diversity of scenes, simulation may help a lot. If it’s handling a delicate object with complicated contact, real experience may matter much more. The useful loop is to train, test on the robot, study the failures, and use those failures to decide what data to collect next.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts simulation’s scale with real data’s expense and describes task-dependent usefulness, but it does not clearly frame the choice as a fixed-budget tradeoff between data quantity and effectiveness at improving the model.

r002.rationale: It says simulator success does not necessarily transfer to the real world and that real experience may matter more for delicate objects with complex contact, conveying that simulated data alone is insufficient for some tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they play complementary roles. Simulation gives you scale: you can try lots of variations, generate failures, and practice things that would be slow or risky on hardware. But real-robot data tells you whether the assumptions in your simulator actually hold. Contact, friction, sensor noise—those details can make a policy that looks great in simulation fail in the real world.

So I wouldn’t pick a fixed ratio. I’d start with the task and ask where the uncertainty is. If it’s broad coverage of environments, simulation can do a lot. If it’s a delicate manipulation task where small physical differences matter, I’d put more weight on real data. The useful loop is to train, test on the robot, understand the failures, and then decide whether you need better simulation or more real experience. Ultimately, I care about how reliably the robot performs on real tasks.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts simulation’s scale with real data’s ability to expose simulator errors, but it does not frame this as quantity versus model-improvement effectiveness within a fixed budget.

r002.rationale: It says simulator policies can fail in the real world because contact, friction, and sensor noise differ, and recommends more real data for delicate manipulation tasks.
